2. Facts giving rise to the Rule are that, petitioner was born in the Bohmong Circle Chiefs family and is a direct descendant in the male line of the Bohmong Chief and that Bandarban Hill District and part of Rangamati Hill District are inhabited by the tribal people of Bohmong Circle having their own way of life and social pattern governed by age old usage, tradition and custom, part of which is to have a chief of the circle appointed from the Bohmong Dynasty. Bohmong Son Byu, being Governor of Chittagong during 1614 to 1630, was the first Bohmong Chief succeeded by other chiefs appointed from the Bohmong dynasty from time to time till 1959. In 1959 on the death of Chief Bohjongree, the 13th Chief, Mong Shwe Prue became the 14th Chief and he died on 16-6-1996 causing a vacancy in the chiefship of the Bohmong circle. Further case of the petitioner is that, the successor of the chief has always been the eldest in the male line, who was not otherwise unfit, and that according to various publications including District Gazetteer, this rule as a custom has been recognised and reported and that the petitioner is grandson of the 9th chief and nephew of 11th Chief and that out of the living male members of Bohmong dynasty petitioner is the senior most in age, whereas the respondent No. 4 Kayw Sain Prue Chowdhury is 3rd in seniority amongst his three brothers all of whom are younger in age to the petitioner and that the petitioner is physically fit and mentally alert and as such, the petitioner is entitled to succeed to the chiefship. But the respondent No. 1 recognised the respondent No. 4 as the Bohmong chief on 4-11-1996 which was published in the official Gazette on 21-11-1996. Being aggrieved by the same petitioner moved this court and obtained the Rule. 

 3. Respondent No. 1 contested the Rule filing an affidavit-in-opposition denying the material allegations made in the application and stating, inter alia, that respondent No.4 is direct descendant from the male line without interruption beginning from the 12th Chief; he is son of the 13th Chief and 14th chief was his paternal uncle and that he is well acquainted with the affairs of Bohmong circle being associated with his late father the 13th chief and that the petitioner is practically distant from the ruling Bohmong Raj family in the affairs of the Bohmong circle's administration and the role of the petitioner during the war of liberation as chairman of the Peace Committee and minister of Malek's cabinet earned him bad reputation and,as such, the respondent No.4 has been appointed by the Government. 

 4. Respondent No.3 also contested the Rule by filing an affidavit-in-opposition denying most of the averments in the writ petition and stating, inter alia, that age alone has not been considered in the past as the only criterion for recognition of the Bohmong Chief. Rather age, fitness, qualification and overall acceptability to the tribal people and quality preserve the dignity of Bohmong chief, loyalty to the Republic, etc. are the determinants for the office of the Bohmong chief and considering all these facts respondent No. 4 is the most appropriate choice and that the respondent No. 4 has got a direct link with the ruling Bohmong chief and the petitioner is not so. Moreover, his role in the war of liberation earned him bad reputation and considering all those factors respondent No. 4 has been recognised as the Bohmong chief. 

 5. Respondent No.4 also contested the Rule by filing an affidavit-in-opposition denying material allegations and reiterating the statements made in the affidavit-in-opposition filed by the respondent No. 1. The respondent No. 4 further stated that while appointing the chief it is the maturity of the claimant and his reasoned mind and not numerical age which is to be considered and after considering the claims of the petitioner and the respondent No.4 vis-a-vis their fitness, age and acceptability Government accorded appointment and recognition in favour of the respondent No. 4. Respondent No. 4 also stated that the petitioner is, in fact, senior to the last 14th chief by 4 days but he was not appointed or recognised as the 14th chief and that the petitioner is not suitable for the appointment and that the members of the Raj family are in favour of appointment and recognition of the respondent No. 4 as the Bohmong chief and that the petitioner is about 81 years old and in the history of three hundred years of Bohmong dynasty no chief was appointed even at the age of seventy and that there being no substance in the Rule it is liable to be discharged. 

 6.On behalf of the petitioner an affidavit-in-reply has been filed against the affidavit- in-opposition filed by the respondent No.4 reiterating the statements made in the writ petition and denying the allegations as to the seniority of the petitioner to the 14th chief and also annexing therewith copy of a letter of the Commissioner, Chittagong Division dated 19-7-1996 recommending the name of the petitioner for the appointment and recognation and as the Bohmong chief and copy of the Gazette notification appointing the 14th chief in 1959. 

 7. Mr. Khandker Mahbubuddin Ahmed, learned Advocate for the petitioner, after placing the materials on record and the impugned notification submitted that the petitioner is senior most in the male line of the dynasty and in view of age old tradition and custom regarding succession to the chief ship of Bohmong circle, his claim ought to have been recognised by the Government. He further submitted that this is not an act of appointment but a mere recognition on the basis of custom and usage which has been disregarded by the Government and the Government issued the impugned notification which is without lawful authority. Mr. Ahmed further submitted that, Commissioner of Chittagong Division weighed the merit for the claimants and recommended the name of the petitioner which has been disregarded by the Government being biased in favour of respondent No. 4 without assigning any reason 'for not accepting the recommendation in favour of the petitioner and, as such, acted illegally in passing the impugned order. 

 8. Mr. KM Saifuddin Ahmed, learned Deputy Attorney-General appearing for the respondent Nos. 1 and 3, after placing the affidavit-in-opposition submitted that age is not the only determining factor for the appointment and recognition of the chief ship. Rather fitness and age together determine the appointment and recognition and that though the petitioner was a state minister in 1979-82 he is a mere matriculate and formerly served as Sub-Inspector of Police earning no promotion and as such, he is not fit to be the chief. Moreover, ie was a collaborator of Pakistan occupation army and detained in custody for 4 years as a collaborator after liberation and, as such, cannot be recognised as the chief. 

 9. Mr. Zakir Ahmed, learned Advocate appearing for the respondent No. 4, has taken us through the Annexures submitted along with affidavit-in-opposition filed by the respondent No. 4 and submitted that Government on consideration of the fitness and age of the respondent No.4 recognised him as the chief. He very strenuously argued that age means maturity and fitness but the petitioner being 82 years old cannot be considered fit for the appointment and recognition as appears from the report of the Deputy Commissioner and that the recommendation of the Commissioner is not binding upon the Government and there is no bar on the part of the Government in not accepting the recommendation of the Commissioner. He also submitted that the members of the Raj family and two wives of the late 14th Chief selected the respondent No.4 for the office and there being no illegality the Rule cannot sustain. 

 10. It appears from notification dated 4-11-1996 that respondent No.4 has been appointed and recognised as the chief of the Bohmong circle of Chittagong Hill Tracts by the Government in exercise of power under Chittagong Hill Tracts Regulations 1900 (Regulation 1 of 1900) and Commissioner of Chittagong Division has been directed to arrange for his investiture under rule 48 made under the aforesaid Chittagong Hill Tracts Regulations. It also appears that succession to the Chiefship of the Bohmong circle is regulated by the custom and usages of the tribal people of the said circle. According to the said custom, a senior male member of the ruling family who is fit to become chief of the tribe is entitled to succeed the deceased chief. Learned Advocate for the petitioner placed much stress on the seniority of a male member of the ruling family and, on the other hand, learned Advocate for the respondents placed much stress on the fitness of the male member of the ruling family for succeeding the late chief of the tribe. Learned Advocate for the petitioner relied on Gazette notification dated 15-8-1959 (Annexure-H to the affidavit-in-reply) by which late Aung Shwe Prue Chowdhury was recognised as the 14th Bohmong chief by the then Government of East Pakistan in support of his contention. On the other hand, learned Advocates for the respondents relied on the letter dated 22-2-1917 issued by the officiating Chief Secretary of the Government of Bengal to the Commissioner of the Chittagong Division printed at pages 350-351 of the book titled "Selections from Correspondence on the Revenue Administration of the Chittagong Hill Tracts" (Annexure-B(4) to the writ petition and Annexurc-1 to the affidavit-in-opposition of the respondent No.4 in support of their contention. It appears from the said notification that late Maung Shew Prue, half-brother of the previous late Bohmong Kaw Zaw Sen was appointed and recognised by the Government as the Bohmong chief as he attained the age of majority and was the senior most and the most experienced amongst the claimants and also the most suitable person. On the other hand, it appears from the said letter that the ruling Bohmong nominated his successor at the time of his investiture and, as such, Government informed the Bohmong chief that such nomination was not acceptable and after examining the principles of succession of Bohmong ship informed the Divisional Commissioner that fitness and age rather than priority of descent regulated succession to the Bohmong ships. 

 11.On consideration of both the documents we find that fitness as well as seniority of the claimants from amongst the male members of the ruling family of the Bohmong circle are to be considered in recognising a person as the chief of the Bohmong circle. In this connection it may be mentioned that there is nothing in the said Regulations or in the Rules made thereunder as to the recognition of the Bohmong chief or chief of any other tribe. Rule 48 only provides that the investiture of the chief is regulated by the Government. Commissioner of the Chittagong Division has overall supervision of the administration of the Chittagong Hill Tracts now divided into 3 Hill districts and under regulations 17 Commissioner may revise any order made under the Regulations by the Deputy Commissioner or any other officer in the Chittagong Hill Tracts. Under regulation 5 Deputy Commissioner appointed by the Government with the help and assistance of Deputy Magistrate and Deputy Collectors and other officers appointed by the Government administer the Hill districts. When a ruling chief of any tribe of the Chittagong Hill Tracts dies Deputy Commissioner concerned of the Hill district recommends the name or names of male member or members from amongst the serving members of the ruling family for recognition as the chief to the Divisional Commissioner who in his turn recommends the name of a surviving male member of ruling family to the Government for such recognition and Government normally accepts such recommendation and recognises the person so recommended as the chief of the tribe concerned and directs the Commissioner of the Division for arranging investiture of such a chief. After such investiture such recognised chief holds the office and dignity of the chief of the tribe. 

 12.It appears from Gazette Notification dated 15-8-1959 that late Aung Shwe Prue succeeded to the office and dignity of the 14th Bohmong chief on the recommendation of the Commissioner of the Chittagong Division that he was the senior-most and most experienced amongst the claimants and most suitable for the said office and dignity of the Bohmong chief. But from the impugned order dated 4-11-1996 we do not find as to whether recommendation of the Commissioner of Chittagong Division was either accepted or rejected by the Government in appointing and recognising the respondent No. 4 as the Bohmong chief after the death of 14th Bohmong chief. It appears from letter dated 19-7-1996 sent by the respondent No.3 Commissioner, Chittagong Division to the Secretary, Special Affairs Division that the Deputy Commissioner Bandarban recommended the names of petitioner as well as respondent No. 4 for nomination and recognition as the chief by the Government but the Commissioner after considering the case of both the persons recommended the name of the petitioner for nomination and recognition as he is the fit, competent and senior most person. It further appears from the said letter that petitioner is not incapacitated or unfit though he is 81 years of age and is more experienced than the respondent No. 4. It further appears from the said letter that some members of the late Bohmong Chief Aung Shwe Prue Chowdhury recommended for recognising respondent No. 4 or Kumar Shwe Aung Prue as the Bohmong chief but the Commissioner opined that there was no custom of nominating the name of any person as the Bohmong chief. It appears from letter dated 7-7-1996 sent by the Deputy Commissioner, Bandarban to the Commissioner of Chittagong Division kept in the Government file and a photostat copy of which has been produced before us for our perusal that, petitioner Aung Shwe Prue Chowdhury is a matriculate, an ex-minister, man of social standing and aged 81 years and respondent No. 4 K yaw Sain Prue Chowdhury is aged 60 years, is an lA, has support of the majority members of the Raj family, an eminent social worker and ex-chairman union parishad and in that perspective Kyaw Sain Prue Chowdhury is physically more able and fit than the petitioner Aung Shwe Prue Chowdhury to discharge the honourous duties of the Bohmong chief. Divisional Commissioner in the aforesaid letter did not find fault with the aforesaid opinion of the Deputy Commissioner but merely opined that the petitioner is not incapacitated or unfit though he was 81 years of age. It appears from summary prepared by the Secretary-in-charge of the Special Affairs Division dated 2-11-1996 photostat copy of which has been produced for our perusal that, substance of the reports of the Deputy Commissioner, Bandarban as well as Commissioner, Chittagong Division were placed before the Prime Minister and the name of respondent No. 4 was suggested for approval of the Prime Minister on the ground that petitioner was a collaborator of the Pakistan occupation army and was a minister of Malek Cabinet in 1971 and was involved in activities prejudicial to the liberation of Bangladesh and he was detained for a long period after liberation as a collaborator and subsequently in 1979 he was elected a member of Parliament and from 1979 to 1982 he was a minister of State in the Cabinet of late Ziaur Rahman and, as such, he was a disputed person. It further appears from the said Summary that it was noticed from the letter of the concerned Deputy Commissioner that the petitioner has no support of the ruling family and the tribal people for being recognised as the chief and respondent No. 4 is one of the senior members of the ruling family and he is an eminent social worker and former chairman of the Union Parishad and he has support of the majority members of the ruling family. The said summary was approved by the Prime Minister on 2-11-1996. Thereafter by Notification dated 4-11-1996 respondent No. 4 was nominated and recognised as the chief of Bohmong circle. 

 13. On consideration of the above materials we find that the Deputy Commissioner, Bandarban forwarded the names of the petitioner and respondent No. 4 to the Commissioner, Chittagong Division but, according to him, respondent No. 4 was more able and fit person than the petitioner to discharge the honors duties of Bohmong chief but the Divisional Commissioner without finding any fault with the said part of the recommendation of the Deputy Commissioner recommended the name of the petitioner as the senior most, competent and fit person for appointment as the Bohmong chief, Government considered both the recommendations and found petitioner as a disputed person having no support of the ruling family and the tribal people. It was further noticed by the Government that this important aspect of the matter was not mentioned by the Divisional Commissioner in his report though the same was pointed out by the Deputy Commissioner concerned in his report to the Divisional Commissioner. Government further found respondent No.4 as one of the senior members of the ruling family and he was an eminent social worker and a former chairman of the Union Parishad and has supported of majority members of the ruling family for nomination and recognition as the Bohmong chief. So the Government did not accept the recommendation of the Divisional Commissioner and recognised the respondent No. 4 as the chief on the grounds mentioned in the said summary. It is well settled that recommendation of a subordinate authority is not binding on the higher authority. Higher authority may accept or reject the same after considering the same if it finds reasons for not accepting the same. 

 14. Ongoing through the letter dated 22-2-1917 issued by the officiating Chief Secretary of Government of Bengal to the Commissioner of Chittagong Division we find that the nomination to the chief ship by the ruling chief was not recognised and after examining the matter the then Government came to the conclusion that chiefship is not transmitted to the eldest surviving male relative by male line of descent and that fitness and age rather than priority of descent regulate succession to the Bohmong chief. Petitioner could not show anything contrary to the said policy decision of the Government which is being followed in nominating and recognising the chief of the Bohmong tribe except the relevant part of the books "An account of the Chittagong Hill Tracts" by Mr. Hutchinson published in 1906 and "District Gazetteers of Chittagong Hill Tracts" published in 1909 by the same author. The said author in those two works opined: "The succession to the tribal chief ship or Bohmong is the next eldest male blood relative and does not follow in the direct line." The then Government having subsequently on examination of the question taken the above policy decision aforesaid opinion of the said author has no force. So we are of the view the succession to Bohmong ship is regulated by fitness and age rather then priority of descent from amongst the male relatives of the ruling family and the eldest surviving male relative by male line of descent cannot succeed the late Bohmong chief on the ground of seniority alone. 

 15. It is true that the Commissioner, Chittagong Division recommended the name of the petitioner as the seniormost member of the ruling family considering his qualification and fitness. But the Deputy Commissioner recommended the name of the respondent No. 4 for such nomination and recognition as the more able and fit person than the petitioner. Without finding any fault with the said part of the Deputy Commissioner's recommendation, Divisional Commissioner made the aforesaid recommendation. On consideration of the summary prepared by the Secretary-in-charge of Special Affairs Division of the Government for consideration of the Prime Minister we find that summary of the report of the Deputy Commissioner as well as Divisional Commissioner was placed before the Prime Minister and it was also mentioned that petitioner was a collaborator and detained for long after liberation as a collaborator though subsequently he was elected as the member of the Parliament and became Minister of State but he had no support of the members of the ruling family and the tribal people, Thus it appears to us that the Government not only considered the report of the Deputy Commissioner and the Divisional Commissioner but also considered the suitability of the respondent No. 4 in preference to the petitioner on politico- administrative consideration. It has already been noticed that there is no provision in the Chittagong Hill Tracts Regulations and the Rules made thereunder as to the recognition of Bohmong chief but there is only mention about investiture under rule 48. Thus it is clear that Bohmong chief is not a holder of any Government post but is a political office and is merely nominated and recognised by the Government from amongst the members of the ruling family considering fitness and age. Fitness has nowhere been defined, There is no mention in the aforesaid policy decision of the Government whether fitness means physical or mental fitness or educational qualification or acceptability of the ruling family or tribal people or acceptability of the Government. Since fitness and age rather than priority of descent regulate succession to the Bohmong chief ship and eldest surviving male relative by male line of descent having no fitness is not entitled to succeed to the Bohmong chief ship, petitioner cannot claim to succeed to the chief ship as the eldest male member of the ruling family unless he is also found fit by the Government. Even the 14th Bohmong chief was not nominated and recognised only on the ground of seniority and experience but also on the ground of suitability. Thus it is clear that suitability of the claimant is also a measure of his fitness for nomination and recognition as the Bohmong chief. Since there is no guideline as to fitness and since the Government found respondent No.4 as a more suitable claimant than the petitioner from amongst the male members of the ruling family on politico-administrative consideration after considering both the reports of the Deputy Commissioner and Divisional Commissioner as noticed above we find no substance in the submissions of the learned Advocate of the petitioner. We, therefore, find no illegality in the impugned order to interfere with the same.
